transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-23
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Havencrest - Head of ML), Maya Singh (Infra Manager), Jordan Price (CISO), Ella Park (Product)

Summary:
Havencrest is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for production LLM inference. Primary drivers: data isolation, predictable throughput for peak hours, cost predictability. Key concerns: SOC2/ISO controls, VPC/private deployment networking, KMS/HSM integration, autoscaling/burst strategy, and questions about kernel/quantization support for their models. Next steps agreed: send pricing, security docs, benchmark run.

Topics: dedicated capacity sizing, reserved GPU tiers, burst capacity and autoscaling, network isolation (VPC/peering), security/compliance, performance benchmarks and pilot timeline.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Alex from Redwood. We got Priya on the line too, our SE. how's everyone doing?
[00:09] Liam O'Connor: Doing good, Alex. Thanks. I know time's tight so we'll try to be concise.
[00:14] Maya Singh: Hi all.
[00:16] Jordan Price: Hey.
[00:18] Alex Chen: Great. Quick agenda: understand current stack and constraints, go over Dedicated offering — reserved GPUs, burst, isolation — and capture success criteria. Priya will run some performance/ops details. Sound good?
[00:28] Ella Park: Yep fine.

[00:31] Alex Chen: Liam, can you give us a quick picture of what you're serving today and why you're considering Dedicated?
[00:38] Liam O'Connor: Sure — so we run a mix of chat and document understanding models. Mostly open weights trimmed — we run at different sizes. Right now it's all on-prem with a home-grown serving layer and some cloud dev env. The pain is peaks in customer support hours — we need predictable latency under 200ms for short prompts and throughput spikes to 500 concurrent requests. Also compliance: logs retention and encryption at rest/key custody are product must-haves.
[01:05] Priya Raman: When you say 200ms, is that p50 or p95?
[01:09] Liam O'Connor: p95 during peak — so we want p95 < 200ms for shorter sequences say up to 256 tokens. Longer seqs can be higher.
[01:16] Priya Raman: Got it. That actually narrows the config a lot.

[01:20] Alex Chen: Jordan, from security perspective what are the non-negotiables?
[01:23] Jordan Price: SOC2 is required, we need KMS integration and HSM support ideally. SAML SSO and RBAC, audit logs, and we need proof of network isolation — VPC peering or private link. Also data residency notes for EU customers. We can't have unvetted third-party access to logs.
[01:37] Alex Chen: Totally. Redwood Dedicated supports customer VPCs, private control plane options for our Private offering, and Dedicated includes customer-managed KMS integrations and audit logging. We'll send the SOC2 and ISO artifacts.

[01:47] Maya Singh: On network: we use an AWS VPC with strict egress rules. If we route to Redwood Dedicated how does peering work? Does traffic ever traverse public internet?
[01:57] Priya Raman: Short answer: no, Dedicated can be deployed into a customer VPC or connected via AWS PrivateLink/peering depending on the mode. Some teams use our managed Dedicated in a partner region where we maintain hardware but traffic is on a private network. We'll clarify the deployment topologies in the doc.

[02:18] Liam O'Connor: Perfect. Now on capacity — we have predictable diurnal patterns with big spikes during 9–11am EST. We want reserved GPUs for steady-state and burst for spikes. How does Redwood handle reserved vs burst?
[02:31] Alex Chen: Dedicated is designed for that. You pick a reserved pool — commit to N GPUs — and then you can configure burst policies to allow overflow onto shared capacity or higher tiers depending on contract. For true isolation you can opt for full reserved fleet with no burst to shared infra. Pricing differs.

[02:48] Ella Park: How do you price burst? Is it per-minute or per-token?
[02:53] Alex Chen: Burst is billed at a higher short-term rate — usually per-minute for GPU capacity or a per-token uplift if we route to a different model family. We'll include concrete examples in the pricing sheet.

[03:05] Priya Raman: Also worth noting that for some workloads, intelligent batching and prefix caching reduce effective qps so you might need fewer GPUs than raw concurrency suggests. We can analyze your prompt mix once you share sample traffic.

[03:20] Liam O'Connor: We'll share sample prompt traces but anonymized. Typical sequences are short — 32–128 tokens — but we do some longer multi-doc summarizations overnight. Would Redwood Dedicated support mixed workloads on the same pool?
[03:33] Priya Raman: Yes, we support multi-model routing and can pin models to subsets of the fleet. For strict isolation each model can be bound to its own node pool. Mixed workloads are fine but you can separate if you want SLA guarantees per model.
[03:47] Jordan Price: On the compliance front, if we do multi-tenant racks or shared burst, who owns the logs and how are they stored?
[03:55] Alex Chen: Customer logs remain under your account and retention policies. Audit logs are exported to your S3 or SIEM over private network. For Dedicated reserved fleet with managed hardware we still ensure separation at the hypervisor and container levels; still, if you need absolute physical isolation we can discuss an on-prem Variant of Private.
[04:15] Maya Singh: On autoscaling: do you do GPU-level autoscale, or is it more request-level load balancing across nodes? We need scaling within a 2-minute window for spikes.
[04:25] Priya Raman: It's a combination. The runtime supports per-node sharding and request-level routing; autoscaling reacts to queue depth and latency signals. We can configure aggressive policies for fast scale-up and more conservative scale-down to avoid oscillation. 2-minute scale-up is achievable but depends on infra cold-starts; if you commit reserved warm nodes, scale is much faster.
[04:48] Liam O'Connor: What's the cold start like when spinning new nodes?
[04:51] Priya Raman: Cold start for a fresh GPU with model load is typically 30–90 seconds depending on model size and quantization. We mitigate with warm standby and model preloading strategies.
[04:59] Ella Park: You mentioned quantization — we use INT8 for cost efficiency. Does Redwood support INT8/FP16? Any caveats?
[05:07] Priya Raman: Yes we support INT8/4-bit quant profiles for supported model families. You might see slight quality changes — we recommend running evals. We also maintain performance profiles per quantization level so we can show expected latency and throughput.
[05:22] Liam O'Connor: What about KV cache and long chat sessions — do you have memory pressure concerns for many concurrent long sessions?
[05:29] Priya Raman: KV cache is handled per-session and we do cache eviction and sharding strategies. For many concurrent long sessions you might need more memory per node; we can recommend node types. Also prefix caching reduces recomputation for repeated prompts.
[05:44] Jordan Price: For keys: our policy requires HSM-backed key custody. Does Redwood integrate with customer HSM or do you have managed HSM?
[05:52] Alex Chen: We integrate with customer KMS/HSM via standard APIs — AWS KMS, external HSMs with KMIP, etc. We'll include specifics in the security doc but integration is supported for Dedicated.
[06:05] Maya Singh: If we do the pilot, what telemetry do we get? We need token-level latency, per-model usage, errors, and cost breakdowns.
[06:13] Priya Raman: Redwood Console gives token-level cost and latency, per-route dashboards, traces, and error analysis. For Dedicated we can increase retention and integrate with your monitoring endpoints (Datadog, Splunk).
[06:26] Liam O'Connor: Cool. On models: we're testing a few community LLMs and a fine-tuned variant. How fast can you onboard a model and what formats do you accept?
[06:36] Priya Raman: We accept typical formats (PyTorch, ONNX, GGUF for quantized weights). Onboarding timeline depends on size and compatibility; small models can be onboarded in days and larger ones in a week or two with perf tuning. We'll run a smoke test and perf profile.
[06:52] Alex Chen: Are there any stakeholders not on this call who need to be engaged? Legal? Procurement?
[06:58] Ella Park: Procurement will want standard enterprise terms, but legal will review after we see security artifacts. Jordan will lead the security review.
[07:07] Jordan Price: We'll need the SOC2 and network diagrams. Also a list of sub-processors and any data flow diagrams.
[07:14] Alex Chen: We'll attach SOC2 and an architecture diagram. Priya can include the data flow diagrams for Dedicated modes.
[07:24] Maya Singh: One technical question — does Redwood support colocated on-prem hardware that we manage but Redwood software orchestrates?
[07:32] Priya Raman: We have a Private on-prem option where the control plane is customer-managed and we provide the orchestration software; that's more of a Private engagement rather than Dedicated managed. For some customers we do a hybrid where compute sits in your DC and we help onboard.
[07:47] Liam O'Connor: For cost predictability, can you outline commitment tiers and what happens if we exceed reserved capacity?
[07:55] Alex Chen: Typical model: monthly or annual reserved commitment with discounted rates. Exceeding reserved capacity triggers burst billing at a premium rate or routes to compatible model variants on shared infra. If you prefer no burst, we can size a fully reserved fleet but that carries higher committed cost. We'll include an example cost sheet for 10/25/50 GPU commitments.
[08:16] Ella Park: Does Redwood do canary rollouts and A/B model testing on Dedicated?
[08:21] Priya Raman: Yes — rollout policies, canaries, A/B, and automatic fallbacks are supported. You can define per-route model priorities and fallbacks in the config.
[08:30] Liam O'Connor: For the pilot, we'd probably start with 8 GPUs reserved and allow 4 GPU burst for peaks. Is that a reasonable starting point?
[08:38] Priya Raman: That sounds reasonable. We'll validate with your real qps and seq distributions. Depending on batching and caching you might need fewer.
[08:45] Jordan Price: A few more security nitpicks: Do you provide tamper-evident logs? Are logs signed?
[08:51] Alex Chen: We provide audit logs and can support log signing/export to your secure storage. We'll capture those requirements in the questionnaire.
[08:58] Maya Singh: How do you handle model drift and updates? If we push a new fine-tuned model can we do a canary to 10% traffic? What's the rollback time?
[09:06] Priya Raman: Yes to canary to 10%. Rollback is typically near instant at the routing layer — milliseconds for routing changes, though model cold-starts might affect TTFB for the first few requests if the new target nodes are cold. For that we do pre-warming.
[09:20] Alex Chen: Anything else from the product side?
[09:23] Ella Park: One question about observability retention: how long do you keep traces by default and can we extend?
[09:29] Priya Raman: Defaults are 30 days for traces and metrics on hosted, but Dedicated allows configurable retention and export. We can extend retention for an add-on.
[09:40] Liam O'Connor: Ok timeline: we want a pilot in July and bulk rollout potentially in Q4. Is that feasible?
[09:47] Alex Chen: Yes — July pilot aligns. We'll need your sample traffic and security answers; Priya will run the perf plan and we'll schedule benchmark windows. Q4 rollout is realistic depending on procurement.
[09:58] Jordan Price: Procurement will want term sheets and SLAs. Do you offer uptime SLA for Dedicated?
[10:04] Alex Chen: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets depending on commitment tier. Higher commitment terms include stricter SLAs and shorter response SLOs. We'll include SLA language and examples.
[10:15] Maya Singh: A quick operational question — who handles OS/kernel updates and model patching for Dedicated managed racks?
[10:23] Priya Raman: For managed Dedicated we handle OS and runtime updates under maintenance windows; for Private or customer-managed compute you handle OS updates. Patching processes are documented and we coordinate with your infra team.
[10:35] Liam O'Connor: For the benchmark phase, what do you need from us?
[10:39] Priya Raman: Sample traffic traces (anonymized), target seq lengths, expected qps during pilot, and model artifacts (or pointers to them). Also a window for running a stress test and an agreed dataset for quality evals.
[10:54] Ella Park: We'll aim to get that to you by Monday.
[10:57] Liam O'Connor: Yep we'll try.
[11:00] Alex Chen: Ok quick recap of next steps: Alex will send pricing and commitment examples and SOC2/architecture docs; Priya will share benchmark guide and perf examples; Jordan will return security questionnaire; Liam to send sample prompts/traffic. We'll set a follow-up to schedule the benchmark.
[11:18] Jordan Price: Sounds good.
[11:20] Ella Park: Thanks Alex, Priya.
[11:22] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with documents and a proposed benchmark window.
[11:30] (end)

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-recognitions present e.g., "Redwood Dedicated" is sometimes transcribed as "Red Wood dedicate", proper nouns may vary.
